analysis.investment_thesis: Nesco is a genuinely fine business — near-monopoly Mumbai exhibition space, virtually no debt, and nine consecutive years of profits — but Mr. Market has priced it at nearly double my Graham Number of ~INR 689 (vs. the current INR 1,208), offering no margin of safety whatsoever. The intelligent investor does not pay a 75% premium over calculated intrinsic value simply because the underlying business is pleasant.
key_strengths: Near-zero debt (D/E 0.04) with interest coverage of ~45x — the balance sheet is a fortress
Nine consecutive years of positive net profits, growing at 11.2% CAGR from INR 144 Cr to INR 375 Cr
Exceptional economics: 85.6% gross margin and 50.9% operating margin signal real pricing power over a captive, near-monopoly asset (BEC)
key_risks: Price grossly exceeds Graham Number: sqrt(22.5 × ~53 EPS × ~397 BVPS) ≈ INR 689 — stock trades at 75% premium
P/B of 3.04 and P/E of 20.8x both violate my strict thresholds; combined P/E × P/B = ~63, far above my 22.5 ceiling
CWIP exploded from INR 162 Cr to INR 761 Cr in one year, turning FCF deeply negative (-INR 435 Cr in 2025) — heavy speculative capital commitment with uncertain returns
red_flags: P/B of 3.04 — paying three times book value for assets I can only value at book
Free cash flow of -INR 435 Cr in 2025 driven by INR 784 Cr capex — earnings no longer covered by cash generation
Other Income of INR 114 Cr (2025) constitutes ~30% of net profit — quality of earnings partially dependent on financial investments, not core operations
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my perspective, Nesco passes the qualitative test handsomely — a real, tangible asset (exhibition centre land in Mumbai), consistent profitability for nearly a decade, and a balance sheet so clean it is almost embarrassing. The operating margin of 51% tells me this business has genuine pricing power; no commodity business earns that. Finance costs of only INR 12 Cr against EBITDA of INR 537 Cr gives interest coverage of 45x — exactly the kind of protective cushion I demand. And promoter ownership at 68.5% aligns management with shareholders.

Yet the price destroys the argument. My Graham Number — the geometric mean of 22.5 times earnings and book value — comes to roughly INR 689. The market demands INR 1,208, a 75% premium. P/E of 20.8 and P/B of 3.04 both breach my hard limits, and their product of ~63 is nearly three times my 22.5 combined ceiling. Worse, the INR 761 Cr in work-in-progress capital (up from INR 162 Cr just one year prior) and a sharply negative 2025 free cash flow signal that management is making a large bet on future expansion — precisely the kind of speculative forward-looking assumption I refuse to pay for today. I do not quarrel with the business; I quarrel with the price.
